theoretical_foundation.description: Four fundamental structures or 'cornerstones of existence' that require continuous dialogical confrontation and exchange

source_quotes.quote: All preconditions of existence can be summarized in four fundamental structures, the 'cornerstones of existence': the world in its factuality and potentiality; life with its network of relationships and its feelings; being oneself as a unique, autonomous person; the wider context where to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future

All preconditions of existence can be summarized in four fundamental structures, the 'cornerstones of existence': • the world in its factuality and potentiality • life with its network of relationships and its feelings • being oneself as a unique, autonomous person • the wider context in which to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future

dialogical_structure.description: Motivation emerges from dialogical exchange between subject and environment
dialogical_structure.source_quote: Motivation is a process of continuous exchange between the subject—individual—and the environment. From an existential perspective, we see this exchange as having a dialogical structure, connecting the given reality of both subject and object with the intentions of the individual.

dialogical_structure.description: Motivation as dialogical movement toward goals
dialogical_structure.source_quote: motivation essentially involves the person (with his or her specific ability to make decisions) in his or her world. Thus, motivation may thus be defined as a process in dialogical movement from the present, given reality towards the person's goals and intentions.

being_in_the_world.source_quote: Seen in that light, the notion of 'being-in-the-world' provides the ground, on which personal forces are activated. This happens by a perceptive encounter with some form of otherness or with oneself.

being_in_the_world.description: Heidegger's concept of Dasein applied to motivation
being_in_the_world.source_quote: Or as Heidegger has defined it: Being a person, 'Dasein', means 'being-in-the-world', means dealing with 'otherness'.

interpersonal_paradigm.description: Dialogical essence of personhood as complement to individualistic paradigm
interpersonal_paradigm.source_quote: We have enlarged our motivational concept by basing it on the most original activity of personhood: Our being essentially dialogical, prone to and directed towards exchange with others. Being oneself, finding oneself needs the field of tension of the 'inter-', the 'between', the 'aida' as the Japanese say

provocation.description: Provocation as starting point for motivation
provocation.source_quote: Being provoked means being called. This provocation is the starting point for any motivation.
We get the necessary provocation through everything which confronts us, which challenges us, which engages us. At exactly that moment the object before us starts 'speaking' to us.

provocation.description: Dialogical beings waiting for completion by partner
provocation.source_quote: As dialogical beings we expect and look for something or someone who 'speaks' to us, calls us, needs us, talks to us, looks for us, challenges us.

FM1_world.subtitle: Dealing with Conditions and Possibilities

existential_question.question: I am—can I be?
existential_question.practical_application: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?

source_quotes.quote: I am—can I be? For making this question practical, I may apply it to my own situation. Then I may ask myself: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?

But I am here, which sets before me the fundamental question of existence: I am – but can I be? To ask a more practical version of this question I need only apply it to my own situation. In that case, I may ask myself: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?

To accept means to be ready to occupy the space, to rely on the support and to trust the protection; in short 'to be there' and not to flee.

To endure means to have the strength to persist in spite of whatever is difficult, menacing or unalterable, and to 'support' what cannot be changed.

procuring_space.source_quote: Human beings procure the space they need with their ability to tolerate and to accept conditions.

FM2_life.name: Second Fundamental Motivation: Life
FM2_life.subtitle: Dealing with Relationships and Emotions
FM2_life.description: Confrontation with the network of relationships and feelings; the pathic dimension of existence

source_quotes.quote: life with its network of relationships and its feelings
life with its network of relationships and its feelings

descriptions.description: Existence is experienced and suffered or enjoyed, not simply happening
descriptions.source_quote: It has a 'pathic dimension,' which means that it does not simply happen, but that we experience and suffer or enjoy it.

descriptions.description: Being alive encompasses the full range of emotional experience
descriptions.source_quote: It has a 'pathic dimension', which means that it does not simply happen, but that we experience and suffer or enjoy it. Being alive means to cry and to laugh, to experience joy and suffering, to go through pleasant and unpleasant things, to be lucky or unlucky and to experience worth and worthlessness. We experience happiness to the same extent and depth that we experience suffering. The amplitude of emotionality is equal in both directions, whether this suits us or not.

existential_question.question: I am alive—do I like this fact?
existential_question.alternative_form: Is it good to be there?

source_quotes.quote: Therefore, I am confronted with the fundamental question of life: I am alive—do I like this fact? Is it good to be there?
Therefore I am confronted with the fundamental question of life: I am alive – but do I like this fact? Is it good to be here?

existential_needs.description: Having relationships where one feels closeness and community

verification_questions.question: Do I have relationships, in which I feel closeness, for which I spend time and in which I experience community?

existential_needs.description: Taking time for valuable things, giving away part of one's life

elaboration.source_quote: To take time for something means to give away a part of one's life while spending it with someone or something.

existential_needs.description: Feeling and maintaining closeness to things, plants, animals, and people

positive_outcomes.description: Experience of being in harmony with the world and oneself

source_quotes.quote: But if these three conditions are fulfilled, I experience myself as being in harmony with the world and with myself, and I can sense the depth of life.

source_quotes.quote: These experiences form the fundamental value, the most profound feeling for the value of life. In each experience of a value this fundamental value is touched upon; it colors the emotions and affects and represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.

These experiences form the fundamental value, the most profound feeling for the inherent value of life. Our experience of any and all values are shaped by this fundamental value, it colors the emotions and affects and represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.

source_quotes.quote: I seize life, engage in it, when I turn to other people, to things, animals, intellectual work or to myself, when I go towards it, get close, get into touch or pull it towards me.

I seize life (carpe diem), engage in it, when I turn toward other people, toward things, animals, intellectual work or to myself, when I move towards it, get close, get in touch or pull it towards me.

existential_question.question: I am myself—may I be like this?
existential_question.alternative_form: Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do?
existential_question.context: The plane of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics

source_quotes.quote: In the midst of this world, I discover myself unmistakably; I am with myself and I am given to myself. This puts before me the fundamental question of being a person: I am myself—may I be like this? Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do?—This is the plane of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics.

In the midst of this world, I discover myself unmistakably, I am with myself and I am given to myself. source_quotes.quote: Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude. Encounter represents the necessary bridge to the other, makes me find his essence as well as my own 'I' in the 'you.'

self_transcendence.description: Need to transcend oneself for fulfillment and fertility
self_transcendence.source_quote: In a sense, we have to transcend ourselves, if we want to find fulfillment in life and to be fertile. Without this self-transcendence, moving beyond ourselves toward something greater, we are condemned to a life of loneliness and triviality.

existential_question.question: I am there—for what is it good?
existential_question.alternative_form: I am here – but for what purpose?
existential_question.context: Recognition of what life is all about; need to transcend oneself for fulfillment

source_quotes.quote: If I can be there, love life and find myself therein, the conditions are fulfilled for the fourth fundamental condition of existence: the recognition of what my life is all about. It does not suffice to simply be there and to have found oneself. In a sense, we have to transcend ourselves, if we want to find fulfillment and to be fruitful... Thus, the transience of life puts before us the question of meaning of our existence: I am there—for what is it good?

source_quotes.quote: But it does not suffice to have a field of activity, to have one's place within a context and to know of values to be realized in the future. Instead, a phenomenological attitude is needed to which we referred at the beginning. descriptions.description: What does this hour want from me, how shall I respond?
descriptions.source_quote: 'What does this hour want from me, how shall I respond?' The meaningful thing is not only what I can expect from life, but, in accordance with the dialogical structure of existence, it is equally important what life wants from me and what the moment expects from me and what I could and should do now for others as well as for myself.

descriptions.description: How am I challenged by this moment, and how should I respond?
descriptions.source_quote: How am I challenged by this moment, and how should I respond? The meaningful thing is not only what I can expect from life, but, in accordance with the dialogical structure of existence, it is equally important what life wants from me. And what the moment expects from me, and what I could and should do now for others as well as for myself.

action_agreement.description: Bringing oneself into agreement with the situation; examining if actions are good

source_quotes.quote: My active part in this attitude of openness is to bring myself into agreement with the situation, to examine whether what I am doing is really a good thing: for others, for myself, for the future, for my environment. If I act accordingly, my existence will be fulfilling.

My active part in this attitude of openness is to bring myself into agreement with the situation, to examine whether what I am doing is really a good thing for others, for myself, for the future, for my environment. If I act accordingly, my existence will be fulfilling.

descriptions.description: The most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which one feels one should decide
descriptions.source_quote: This notion of valuable possibilities endorsed with the theory of the fundamental existential motivations, defines meaning even more concretely as 'the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself.'

descriptions.description: What is possible here and now on basis of facts and reality
descriptions.source_quote: This notion of valuable possibilities, endorsed by the theory of the fundamental existential motivations, defines meaning even more concretely as the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself. Existential meaning is therefore what is possible here and now, on the basis of facts and reality, what is possible for me, may it be what I need now, or what is the most pressing, valuable or interesting alternative now.

frankl_definition.description: A possibility against the background of reality

source_quotes.quote: Viktor Frankl (1987, p. 315) once defined meaning as 'a possibility against the background of reality.'
VIKTOR FRANKL (1987, 315) once defined meaning as 'a possibility against the background of reality'.

organ_of_perception.description: Internal ability to reduce complexity of meaning-finding
organ_of_perception.source_quote: To define and redefine this continually is an extremely complex task, which requires an internal 'organ of perception' or ability capable of reducing this complexity to livable proportions: Our sensitivity as well as our moral conscience.

descriptions.description: Overall meaning independent of the individual; philosophical and religious meaning
descriptions.source_quote: Besides this existential meaning, there is an ontological meaning. This is the overall meaning in which I find myself and which does not depend on me. It is the philosophical and religious meaning, the meaning the creator of the world must have had in mind.

Apart from this existential meaning we may also consider an ontological meaning. This is the overall meaning in which I find myself and which does not depend on me. It is the philosophical and religious meaning, the meaning the creator of the world must have had in mind. I can perceive it in presentiments and in faith

steps.name: Recognizing
steps.description: Recognizing something in its worth or value, as it speaks to us

source_quotes.quote: Recognizing something in its worth or value, insofar as it speaks to us. This is often a challenge demanding action on our part. To see what a situation provokes in us means to recognize the situational meaning involved.

Recognizing something in its worth or value, in as far as it speaks to us. This is often a challenge demanding action on our part. What a situation 'pro-'vokes in us is indicative of or points to the situational meaning involved. To recognize this inner movement lays way to find personal meaning.

steps.name: Harmonizing
steps.description: Bringing perceived value into accordance with inner reality

source_quotes.quote: Harmonizing. Bringing the perceived value, challenge or meaning into accordance with one's inner reality, i.e., examining the consistency with the rest of our values, with attitudes, abilities and capabilities and with our conscience.

Harmonizing. Bringing the perceived value, challenge or meaning into accordance with our inner reality (i.e. examining the congruence with the rest of our values, with attitudes, abilities and capabilities and with our conscience etc.).

steps.name: Inner consent
steps.description: Inner consent to one's own active involvement, bringing presence of the inner person

source_quotes.quote: The final step in the development of motivation is the inner consent to one's own active involvement. This consent and the act of harmonizing the new value with inner (already existing personal) reality leads to the presence of the inner person in one's actions. It brings up the integration of the new value and the person himself into a wider context (meaning).

Giving inner consent to one's own active involvement. This consent and the act of harmonizing the new value with one's personal reality lead to the presence of the inner person in one's actions and to the integration of the new value and the person into a wider context (meaning).

omitting_person.description: Without person's involvement, there is only reflex or reaction, not action
omitting_person.source_quote: Omitting the person in the motivational process, according to our opinion, misses the main thrust of human motivation. Instead it focuses on a sort of reflex or reaction, but no 'action'. Any act or deed is defined as a decided act and is therefore voluntary and free.

coding_guidelines.application: Use this codebook to identify and code participant testimony related to the four fundamental motivations
coding_guidelines.hierarchical_structure: Code using FM1-FM4 as primary domains, with sub-codes for needs, outcomes, and actions
coding_guidelines.temporal_analysis: Consider participant experiences before, during, and after therapeutic intervention
coding_guidelines.exclusion_criteria: Only code content that directly relates to the described themes with supporting evidence from source materials

version_notes.v3.0: Initial codebook based on Längle (2011). Includes all four fundamental motivations with existential questions, needs, positive/negative outcomes, active participation elements, motivational process steps, and structure of will.
version_notes.v3.1: Integrated Längle (2003). Added: expanded theoretical foundation with being-in-the-world, interpersonal paradigm, provocation concept; refined motivational process descriptions; expanded FM2 with carpe diem and life reverberation; added histrionic disorders and suicidal tendencies to negative outcomes; expanded FM4 with self-transcendence emphasis and organ of perception for meaning; enhanced all four FMs with additional source quotes and refined descriptions.
